claims.text: Refractory HEAs retain toughness when grain-boundary precipitates remain fine, coherent, and discontinuous.
Thermal exposure causes toughness loss by coarsening grain-boundary precipitates into continuous, brittle intermetallic networks.
The morphology of grain-boundary precipitates governs crack arrest and ductility.
TaNbHfZrTi can initially possess a predominantly BCC structure before secondary-phase formation.
The proposed initial refractory HEA has fine grains and baseline toughness.
Controlled aging at different temperatures and durations will modify the morphology and distribution of grain-boundary precipitates.
Below approximately 1000°C, diffusion-driven precipitation occurs in the relevant refractory HEAs.
Thermal exposure promotes diffusion-induced segregation at grain boundaries.
Lower aging temperatures or shorter aging times produce fine, coherent grain-boundary precipitates.
Fine, coherent precipitates act as dislocation sinks.
Fine, coherent precipitates reinforce grain boundaries without impairing ductility.
Higher aging temperatures or longer aging times cause precipitates to coarsen and form continuous grain-boundary networks.
Continuous precipitate networks act as stress concentrators that facilitate crack initiation and propagation.
Lower-temperature or shorter-duration aging will cause only minimal toughness degradation relative to an as-cast baseline.
Higher-temperature or longer-duration aging will produce coarse, continuous grain-boundary precipitates.
Formation of coarse, continuous grain-boundary precipitates will coincide with lower fracture toughness, impact energy, and ductility.
The proposed behavior applies broadly to thermomechanically processed refractory HEAs exposed below approximately 1000°C.
Failure to observe a statistically significant decrease in toughness and ductility after coarse, continuous precipitates develop would falsify the hypothesis.
